paragraphs: This paper studies what neural networks learn by modeling their internal representations probabilistically. It uses Bayesian nonparametric models to describe activations in convolutional networks and latent representations in variational autoencoders. These models provide a tractable measure of activation complexity and a way to examine the overall structure of a learned latent space.

For convolutional networks, the authors compare representations associated with learning useful patterns and memorizing data. Networks able to exploit patterns develop substantially less complex representations than networks forced to memorize. The analysis also distinguishes two regularization methods: input augmentation and dropout affect representation complexity differently, with dropout’s effects depending strongly on network width.

For autoencoders, increasing regularization makes the aggregated posterior of standard beta-VAEs rapidly approach the diagonal prior. MMD-based variants retain richer posterior distributions under strong regularization, but their latent dimensions do not exhibit independence. The authors also use their probabilistic models to sample latent codes, improving generated sample quality for VAEs with rich posteriors. Together, these findings connect representation complexity, regularization, and sampling behavior.
neurips-2020-a-bayesian-nonparametrics-v.tldr: Probabilistic models of neural representations reveal how memorization and regularization affect complexity and improve sampling from VAEs with rich posteriors.

paragraphs: Compositional zero-shot recognition asks a model to recognize combinations of familiar components that it has not encountered together during training. The challenge is that training data can encourage shortcuts: a feature may correlate with a category without being essential to it. When familiar attributes and objects appear in new combinations, those correlations can produce systematic mistakes.

The paper frames this problem using causal reasoning. It proposes interpreting recognition as asking which intervention produced the observed image. Building on that perspective, the authors introduce an embedding model that learns separate representations of elementary visual components from training data in which those components are correlated. This separation is intended to support recombining what the model has learned.

The approach is evaluated on attribute-object prediction using controlled synthetic images and a real-world dataset of fine-grained shoe categories. It improves over strong baselines in those evaluations. The contribution combines a causal interpretation of compositional recognition with a concrete representation-learning method, providing evidence that separating components can help recognition transfer to previously unseen combinations.
neurips-2020-a-causal-view-of-compositio.tldr: A causally inspired model learns separated visual components and improves recognition of unseen attribute-object combinations on two datasets.

paragraphs: Adversarial learning often proceeds through alternating advances: a new attack defeats a defense, and a new defense addresses that attack. This paper asks whether that process can reach an equilibrium where neither side can improve by changing its strategy alone. It develops a game-theoretic framework for analyzing attacks and defenses together.

The main result depends on a specific model of the classifier. For a binary classifier whose decision boundary is locally linear, the authors prove that a Fast Gradient Method attack and a Randomized Smoothing defense form a Nash equilibrium. Within that modeled game, each is an appropriate response to the other. The local linearity assumption is central to the stated conclusion.

The paper also addresses how to approximate the equilibrium defense using finitely many samples from the distribution generating the data. It derives a generalization bound for this approximation, connecting the equilibrium analysis to a defense constructed from limited observations. The contribution therefore includes both a conditional equilibrium result and an analysis of how its approximation performs beyond the available samples.
neurips-2020-a-game-theoretic-analysis-o.tldr: Under a locally linear binary-classifier model, Fast Gradient Method and Randomized Smoothing form a Nash equilibrium with a finite-sample defense approximation.

paragraphs: Optimistic reinforcement learning encourages exploration by treating uncertain possibilities favorably. Two common approaches apply this idea differently: one constructs an optimistic model of the environment, while the other uses optimistic values during dynamic programming. This paper develops a shared framework for these approaches in reinforcement learning problems organized into episodes.

Using Lagrangian duality, the authors show that every model-optimistic algorithm that constructs an optimistic Markov decision process has an equivalent value-optimistic dynamic-programming representation. This matters because the two approaches were commonly associated with different advantages. Model-based optimism offered cleaner probabilistic analysis, while value-based optimism was considered easier to implement.

The framework yields a class of algorithms combining efficient dynamic-programming implementations with simple probabilistic analyses. It captures many existing algorithms for tabular problems, where states and actions can be represented explicitly. It also extends to larger problems under realizable function approximation, enabling model-based analyses of some recently proposed methods. The result provides a common language for designing algorithms and understanding connections between methods previously treated as distinct.
neurips-2020-a-unifying-view-of-optimism.tldr: Lagrangian duality connects model-based and value-based optimism, enabling efficient episodic reinforcement learning algorithms with simpler analyses.

paragraphs: Contextual linear bandit algorithms must balance learning about available actions with choosing actions that yield good rewards. The paper starts from the observation that optimism-based approaches can miss useful problem structure and be asymptotically suboptimal. It instead designs an algorithm around problem-dependent lower bounds on regret, the loss associated with learning rather than always choosing optimally.

The authors reformulate the lower bound to separate the context distribution from the exploration policy, producing an approach robust to uneven context frequencies. An incremental primal-dual method solves a relaxed optimization problem efficiently. The algorithm also replaces forced exploration with exploration encouraged through confidence intervals for that optimization problem, adapting the required learning effort to problem structure.

The paper proves asymptotic optimality and supplies both problem-dependent and worst-case finite-time regret guarantees. Its bounds depend logarithmically on the number of arms, avoiding the linear dependence reported for related prior work. Minimax optimality at every learning horizon is established specifically for non-contextual linear bandits. Experiments additionally show better performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered.
neurips-2020-an-asymptotically-optimal-p.tldr: An incremental primal-dual bandit algorithm achieves asymptotic optimality while adapting exploration to context frequencies and problem structure.

paragraphs: SATNet combines a logical solver with a differentiable neural-network layer, allowing logical reasoning to participate in learning. Its reported success on visual Sudoku suggested progress toward systems that connect image recognition with symbolic reasoning. This paper investigates whether that success also demonstrates learning the connection between visual inputs and the symbols used by the solver.

The authors remove intermediate labels that identify digit images with their logical representations. Under that condition, SATNet achieves zero test accuracy on visual Sudoku. They attribute the failure to symbol grounding: learning which perceptual patterns correspond to which symbols. This experiment distinguishes solving a logical problem with supplied symbol associations from learning those associations as part of the task.

The paper also proposes a simpler MNIST-based grounding test as a sanity check for differentiable symbolic solvers. Naive uses of SATNet perform worse on this test than models without logical reasoning capabilities. The authors investigate causes and ways to prevent the failures. The findings clarify which capability the earlier visual Sudoku result established and why evaluating the perceptual-to-symbolic connection separately matters.
neurips-2020-assessing-satnet-s-ability-.tldr: SATNet fails visual Sudoku without intermediate digit-to-symbol labels, motivating a simpler test of symbol grounding.

paragraphs: Attention modules strengthen visual networks by changing the emphasis placed on spatial locations or feature channels. Designing how these operations interact can demand substantial computation and expertise. Auto Learning Attention, or AutoLA, addresses that design problem by automatically searching for an attention module’s structure.

The authors introduce high order group attention, called HOGA, and represent it as a directed acyclic graph. Groups form the graph’s nodes, while connections represent different attention operations. A differentiable search method chooses an architecture within this representation. Using a ResNet-20 backbone on CIFAR10, the reported search for a typical HOGA module takes no more than one GPU day.

The resulting module can be inserted into different network backbones as a reusable component. Evaluations cover image classification on CIFAR100 and ImageNet, plus object detection and human keypoint detection on COCO. The searched module outperforms popular manually designed spatial and channel attention modules across the reported tasks. These findings support automatic attention design as a way to discover structures that remain useful beyond the original search setting.
neurips-2020-auto-learning-attention-730.tldr: AutoLA automatically searches attention structures that transfer across network backbones and outperform popular handcrafted attention modules on several vision tasks.

paragraphs: Regularization helps a supervised model make predictions on examples beyond its training data. CASTLE introduces causal structure into this process by jointly learning relationships among variables while training a neural network. The motivation is that the direction of a relationship can matter for prediction, whereas conventional regularizers generally do not account for causality.

The method represents a causal directed acyclic graph through an adjacency matrix embedded in the network’s input layers. Learning this structure becomes an auxiliary part of learning the predictor. CASTLE also uses the graph to determine which input features to reconstruct: it reconstructs features with a causal neighbor, rather than requiring reconstruction of every input feature.

This selective reconstruction ties the regularization objective to the relationships discovered among variables. The paper provides a theoretical generalization bound and evaluates the method on synthetic and publicly available real datasets. CASTLE consistently improves out-of-sample prediction relative to the benchmark regularizers in those experiments. The contribution is therefore a concrete way to incorporate causal graph learning into regularization, supported by both analysis and predictive evaluations.
neurips-2020-castle-regularization-via-a.tldr: CASTLE regularizes neural networks through joint causal graph learning and selective feature reconstruction, improving predictions on the evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops algorithms for maximizing monotone continuous submodular functions under a linear constraint. The goal is to obtain a guaranteed fraction of the best achievable objective value. The authors present the first continuous optimization algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for this setting, extending the scope indicated by the paper’s focus beyond DR-submodularity.

The first method, COORDINATE-ASCENT+, modifies ordinary coordinate ascent. It guarantees an approximation factor of (e−1)/(2e−1) minus epsilon and uses O(n/epsilon) iterations, where n is the problem dimension. Each iteration has roughly O(n/sqrt(epsilon) + n log n) computational cost. Epsilon controls how closely the guarantee approaches the stated constant.

The second method, COORDINATE-ASCENT++, improves the approximation factor to the tight value 1−1/e minus epsilon while retaining the same iteration count. Its total work per iteration is substantially higher, but each round can be parallelized so that the cost per machine matches the first method’s stated scaling. The results make explicit a trade-off between approximation quality and computation, including how parallel execution can distribute the more demanding method’s work.
neurips-2020-continuous-submodular-maxim.tldr: Two coordinate-ascent algorithms provide constant-factor guarantees for constrained continuous submodular maximization, trading more computation for a tight approximation.

paragraphs: Modeling several random variables together requires describing both their individual distributions and their dependence on one another. Copulas separate these tasks by representing dependence through a joint cumulative distribution with uniform marginals. This paper brings that statistical approach into a differentiable neural architecture designed for the Archimedean family of copulas.

The proposed architecture, ACNet, enforces structural properties needed to learn this family. Its target is a copula generator, a mathematical object that implicitly determines the joint cumulative distribution function. This differs from directly learning a density or a data-generation process. The architecture therefore places neural learning inside a structured representation of statistical dependence.

The authors provide a probabilistic interpretation of ACNet’s parameters and use it to derive a simple, efficient sampling algorithm for the learned copula. Experiments show that ACNet can approximate common Archimedean copulas and construct new ones that may fit data better. The findings support a flexible way to learn dependence while preserving the structure of the chosen copula family, with sampling available from the resulting model.
neurips-2020-deep-archimedean-copulas-06.tldr: ACNet learns structurally valid Archimedean copulas and supports efficient sampling, with learned copulas that may fit data better.

paragraphs: Crowd-counting datasets commonly mark each person with a single dot. Many methods transform those sparse annotations into training targets by spreading each dot into a Gaussian shape. This paper argues that imposing those shapes harms generalization and introduces DM-Count, a method that compares distributions without requiring that smoothing step.

DM-Count uses optimal transport to measure similarity between the normalized predicted density map and the normalized ground-truth map. This gives the training objective a way to compare how density is distributed across an image. The model also includes a total variation loss to stabilize the optimal-transport computation. Together, these choices define a distribution-matching approach to learning from point annotations.

The authors derive a tighter generalization-error bound than for Gaussian-smoothed methods. Empirically, DM-Count improves mean absolute error by a large margin on UCF-QNRF and NWPU and achieves state-of-the-art results on ShanghaiTech and UCF-CC50. The abstract also reports an approximately 16% error reduction over a published state-of-the-art result. The theoretical and empirical findings both support reconsidering how dot annotations are converted into supervision.
neurips-2020-distribution-matching-for-c.tldr: DM-Count replaces Gaussian-smoothed supervision with optimal-transport distribution matching, improving crowd-counting results and the stated generalization bound.

paragraphs: Voting rules are often justified through axioms expressing desirable properties of collective decisions. Those same axioms can also be used to explain why a particular voting outcome follows. This paper examines a practical obstacle for that approach: even a logically valid explanation could be too long to be useful.

For the Borda voting rule, the authors prove that outcomes can be explained in O(m²) steps, where m is the number of alternatives. This supplies a concrete upper bound on explanation length. It establishes how the required number of steps scales as the set of alternatives grows, addressing the previously unresolved possibility of excessively lengthy explanations.

The paper’s main technical result is a general lower bound that makes the Borda upper bound asymptotically tight. Thus, in the analyzed framework, the quadratic scaling cannot generally be improved in its order of growth. The authors discuss possible implications for AI and machine learning, including virtual democracy. Their contribution establishes limits on the length of axiom-based explanations, giving a mathematical basis for assessing their potential practicality.
neurips-2020-explainable-voting-d0971500.tldr: Borda voting outcomes admit axiom-based explanations of quadratic length, and a matching lower bound establishes that scaling as asymptotically tight.

paragraphs: Binary-code quantization represents neural-network weights using bits that can participate directly in computation. Earlier approaches restricted the number of quantization bits to integers, limiting the available trade-offs between model size and accuracy. FleXOR expands this design space by compressing quantized weights to achieve fractional numbers of stored bits per weight, including averages below one.

The method uses an encoding and decoding architecture built around XOR operations. During inference, digital XOR-gate networks inserted into the model decode the compressed representation. During training, the gates are described using tanh so gradients can be calculated. This lets training determine both quantization choices and the encoded bit decisions that support compression.

Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet show that the inserted gates can learn these decisions while retaining high accuracy, including with fractional sub-one-bit weights. The paper reports smaller models and higher accuracy than binary neural networks. Its central contribution is making fractional storage budgets trainable through a decoder that is part of the network, rather than restricting compression choices to whole bits per weight.
neurips-2020-flexor-trainable-fractional.tldr: FleXOR learns XOR-based compressed weight encodings that achieve fractional bits per weight with favorable size and accuracy results.

paragraphs: Sequence models need to summarize an expanding history while processing new observations incrementally. HiPPO formulates that memory problem as online approximation: it compresses a continuous signal or discrete time series by projecting its history onto polynomial bases. A measure specifies how much importance to assign to different past times.

Given that measure, HiPPO provides an optimal solution to the resulting approximation problem. The framework derives the Legendre Memory Unit from first principles and generalizes recurrent-network gating mechanisms. It also yields HiPPO-LegS, a memory update that scales with time to represent the full history without choosing a prior timescale. Its theoretical properties include timescale robustness, fast updates, and bounded gradients.

When incorporated into recurrent networks, these memory dynamics empirically capture complex temporal dependencies. HiPPO-LegS achieves 98.3% accuracy on permuted MNIST, reported as a new state of the art. It also outperforms recurrent-network and neural-ODE baselines on a trajectory task testing unfamiliar timescales and missing data. The framework connects an explicit mathematical memory objective to practical sequence-learning behavior.
neurips-2020-hippo-recurrent-memory-with.tldr: HiPPO derives recurrent memory from optimal polynomial approximation and yields a timescale-robust update with strong sequence-learning results.

paragraphs: Finding an effective treatment can require trying several options, making the sequence of trials part of the problem. This paper formalizes the goal as learning a policy that finds a near-optimal treatment using as few trials as possible. The objective explicitly connects treatment quality with the effort required to discover a suitable option.

The authors develop a model-based dynamic-programming algorithm within a causal inference framework. It learns from observational data and is described as robust to unmeasured confounding. They also propose a greedy alternative to reduce computational complexity. That alternative bounds the near-optimality constraint, linking the simplified search procedure to the requirement that the selected treatment be sufficiently effective.

Evaluations use synthetic data and real-world healthcare data, with model-free reinforcement learning as a comparison. The proposed methods compare favorably in those evaluations while making the trade-off between search length and treatment efficacy more transparent. The contribution is a way to study treatment selection as a sequential causal search problem, where avoiding unnecessary trials and finding an effective treatment are jointly represented in the objective.
neurips-2020-learning-to-search-efficien.tldr: Causal treatment-search algorithms learn from observational data to balance fewer trials against finding a near-optimal treatment.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition involves many examples of some classes and few examples of others. Rebalancing becomes especially difficult when multiple classes appear together in the same image. This paper develops a causal account of the problem, aiming to explain existing reweighting and resampling methods and derive a more principled solution.

Within the authors’ framework, momentum in stochastic gradient descent acts as a confounder with two different effects. One pushes predictions for rare classes toward frequent classes. Another, mediated effect helps representation learning and prediction for frequent classes. This distinction motivates separating momentum’s influences rather than treating its contribution as uniformly harmful.

The method targets the direct causal effect of an input sample, using causal intervention during training and counterfactual reasoning during inference. Its aim is to remove the harmful influence while retaining the beneficial one. The paper reports new state-of-the-art results on long-tailed CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, ImageNet-LT, and LVIS. These evaluations cover both image classification and instance segmentation, supporting the proposed approach across the reported long-tailed visual recognition settings.
neurips-2020-long-tailed-classification-.tldr: A causal framework separates helpful and harmful momentum effects to improve long-tailed visual recognition.

paragraphs: Learning a repeating pattern involves more than matching observations within the training range. A model must also continue the repetition when asked to predict beyond that range. This paper studies that extrapolation problem and examines why neural networks with commonly used activation functions struggle with simple periodic functions.

The authors provide proofs and experiments showing failures of periodic extrapolation for ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, and their variants. They hypothesize that these failures arise because the activations lack a periodic inductive bias: their structure does not encourage continuation of a repeating pattern. That explanation is presented as a hypothesis motivating the proposed modification.

The proposed activation is x + sin²(x), which combines a linear term with a repeating component. The authors describe it as providing the desired periodic bias while retaining a favorable optimization property associated with ReLU-based activations. They apply the method experimentally to temperature and financial prediction. The contribution connects extrapolation behavior to activation design and supplies a concrete architectural change intended to make periodic structure easier to learn.
neurips-2020-neural-networks-fail-to-lea.tldr: The paper studies failures of periodic extrapolation and proposes x + sin²(x) as an activation with a periodic inductive bias.

paragraphs: No-regret learning has a known connection to the long-run frequency of actions in finite games: those frequencies approach the set of coarse correlated equilibria. That statement leaves a different question open. It does not establish whether players’ actual, day-to-day strategies settle near a Nash equilibrium.

This paper studies that question for follow the regularized leader, or FTRL, a widely studied family of no-regret learning dynamics. The authors prove that a Nash equilibrium cannot be both stable and attracting under FTRL unless it is strict. Strictness means that each player has a unique best response at the equilibrium.

Because strict Nash equilibria are pure, the result rules out mixed Nash equilibria as stable attracting outcomes of these dynamics. The conclusion concerns which equilibria can serve as stable limiting behavior; it does not assert that learning always converges to a strict equilibrium. This distinction matters when using equilibrium concepts to predict the outcome of repeated learning: guarantees about aggregate frequencies do not supply the same prediction as guarantees about the evolving strategies themselves.
neurips-2020-no-regret-learning-and-mixe.tldr: Under FTRL dynamics, only strict, and therefore pure, Nash equilibria can be stable attracting limits.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernels provide a way to study massively overparameterized neural networks through kernel regression. This paper investigates how the neural tangent kernel of a fully connected ReLU network relates to the familiar Laplace kernel. The comparison asks whether a simpler mathematical object can capture important properties of the network-associated kernel.

For normalized data on a hypersphere, the authors prove that the two kernels have identical eigenfunctions and eigenvalues that decay polynomially at the same rate. Consequently, their reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces contain the same sets of functions. In plain terms, they support function classes with the same smoothness properties under this normalization condition.

The kernels differ away from the hypersphere, but experiments indicate that these differences have little significance when data is properly normalized. Real-data comparisons also find nearly identical performance for the neural tangent kernel, the Laplace kernel, and a broader family of gamma-exponential kernels. The results suggest that analyzing the Laplace kernel’s simple closed form can provide insight into neural networks through this established kernel connection.
neurips-2020-on-the-similarity-between-t.tldr: For data on a hypersphere, the ReLU neural tangent kernel and Laplace kernel support the same function sets and show similar empirical performance.

paragraphs: Reliable prediction requires representing uncertainty, including uncertainty associated with the data and with what the model has learned. Sampling predictions from dropout variants or ensembles can make inference slow. Another approach predicts distributions over class probabilities directly, but prior methods described here require arbitrary target parameters and access to out-of-distribution examples during training.

Posterior Network, or PostNet, uses normalizing flows to produce a closed-form posterior distribution over predicted probabilities for each input. This represents uncertainty about the probability prediction itself. Crucially, the method learns without requiring out-of-distribution training samples, addressing a dependency that is difficult to satisfy when future unfamiliar inputs are unknown.

The paper reports that the learned posterior distributions accurately reflect uncertainty for both familiar and out-of-distribution inputs. It also reports state-of-the-art results in detecting out-of-distribution examples and calibrating uncertainty under dataset shifts. The central contribution is an input-specific posterior construction that supports uncertainty estimation without supplying examples of the unfamiliar data it will later need to recognize.
neurips-2020-posterior-network-uncertain.tldr: PostNet uses normalizing flows to estimate predictive uncertainty without out-of-distribution training data, achieving strong detection and calibration results.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings of a black-box function when evaluating each candidate is expensive. As the number of parameters increases, retaining efficiency in the number of evaluations becomes difficult. One proposed remedy is to conduct the search through a lower-dimensional representation, often constructed using a random linear embedding.

This paper reexamines how such embeddings are used. The authors study properties of existing approaches and identify important issues and misconceptions, showing that some design choices reduce performance. This shifts attention from the general promise of dimensionality reduction to the particular choices involved in building an embedding-based optimization method.

The authors then address those issues and evaluate the resulting approach on a range of problems, including learning a gait policy for robot locomotion. Their experiments show substantial improvements in the effectiveness of linear embeddings for Bayesian optimization. The findings suggest that the practical value of an embedding depends strongly on its design and use: correcting problematic choices can improve performance while retaining the underlying strategy of searching through a lower-dimensional representation.
neurips-2020-re-examining-linear-embeddi.tldr: Revisiting problematic design choices substantially improves linear-embedding Bayesian optimization on evaluated problems, including robot gait learning.

paragraphs: This paper constructs a quantum recurrent neural network for tasks that require processing inputs over time. Its recurrent cell uses parameterized quantum neurons together with amplitude amplification. These components create nonlinear activations involving polynomials of the current input and hidden state, and allow a distribution over predicted classes to be extracted at each step.

To study training, the authors provide a PyTorch implementation that supports relatively efficient optimization of quantum circuits with tens of thousands of parameters. They benchmark optimization settings and examine network structures for memorization and sequence prediction. In these investigations, the model does not appear to suffer from the vanishing-gradient problem affecting many quantum classifiers and classical recurrent networks.

The authors also evaluate classification by feeding MNIST images to the model one pixel at a time. A network using 12 qubits achieves more than 98% test accuracy when distinguishing digits zero and one. This result concerns that two-digit task. Together, the experiments demonstrate a recurrent quantum construction capable of nontrivial sequence learning and classification, alongside a setup for studying its optimization.
neurips-2020-recurrent-quantum-neural-ne.tldr: A quantum recurrent network demonstrates sequence learning and exceeds 98% accuracy on pixel-by-pixel MNIST zero-versus-one classification using 12 qubits.

paragraphs: Worst-case results show that learning deep networks can be computationally hard even when the goal is only slightly better prediction than random guessing. Yet small patches of natural images often contain information about the label, making this weak form of learning straightforward. The paper examines when that local information can support substantially stronger learning.

The authors define a distributional property called local correlation. It requires correlations with the target label in small patches of the input and in intermediate layers of the target function. This requirement goes beyond finding a useful clue in the original image: informative local structure must also occur within the function being learned.

The paper empirically demonstrates this property on CIFAR and ImageNet. Its main theoretical result proves that, for certain classes of deep functions, weak learning implies efficient strong learning under the local-correlation assumption. The restriction matters because weak-to-strong learning implications do not automatically carry over to distribution-specific settings. The result identifies a concrete condition under which locally informative structure can bridge that gap for the studied function classes.
neurips-2020-the-implications-of-local-c.tldr: For certain deep function classes, local correlations with labels are sufficient to turn weak learning into efficient strong learning.

paragraphs: L1 regularization is widely used to encourage sparse models, in which many parameters are zero. Solving the resulting optimization problems requires dealing with a nonsmooth objective. Existing efficient algorithms exploit the problems’ convexity and sparsity, but the usefulness of those approaches can depend on how sparse the solution is and how accurately it must be computed.

Thunder introduces an active incremental approach to improve solver efficiency. The paper presents it as a coordinate-selection solver, placing the choice of coordinates to work on at the center of the method. Its aim is to improve computation for sparse learning, including demanding cases where existing methods struggle.

The authors report that the method performs well when solutions have relatively low sparsity or when high solution accuracy is required. They support its advantages with theoretical analysis and experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. These findings matter because a solver’s practical usefulness depends on more than performance in strongly sparse, moderate-accuracy settings. Thunder targets efficiency across cases that challenge methods relying heavily on favorable sparsity.
neurips-2020-thunder-a-fast-coordinate-s.tldr: Thunder improves L1-regularized optimization with active incremental coordinate selection, including cases with limited sparsity or demanding accuracy requirements.

paragraphs: Scenes with a wide range of brightness can produce overexposed or underexposed regions in conventional cameras. Modulo cameras offer a different route to high dynamic range, but their images must be unwrapped to recover brightness information. Earlier unwrapping based on Markov random fields degrades under intensity ambiguity, strong local contrast, and color misalignment.

UnModNet reformulates this reconstruction problem as a sequence of binary labeling tasks. Its modulo edge-aware model repeatedly estimates binary rollover masks, which guide the unwrapping of the recorded image. This breaks the reconstruction into successive decisions about rollovers while using edge information in the estimation process.

Experiments show that the approach can reliably reconstruct 12-bit high-dynamic-range images from 8-bit modulo images. It also runs substantially faster than the previous Markov-random-field method, with the speed advantage attributed to GPU acceleration. The contribution is both a reformulation of modulo unwrapping and a learned model for carrying it out, demonstrating practical reconstruction at the reported bit depths despite difficulties associated with earlier unwrapping methods.
neurips-2020-unmodnet-learning-to-unwrap.tldr: UnModNet iteratively predicts rollover masks to reconstruct 12-bit HDR images from 8-bit modulo images faster than the previous MRF-based approach.
